column1: # The rows of the third formalizer run, from ANSI/AISC 360-22: requirements the standard states in
# prose, lines of tables that are formulas, one footnote that changes a tabulated value, one table,
# and three equations. Each was transcribed twice from images of the printed pages, by transcribers
# that saw neither each other's rows nor any worked example.
# a3.json and b3.json are the two transcriptions as made, and examples3.json the worked examples as a
# third agent collected them from the Design Examples v16.0. The two transcribers were two different
# models this time (the first two runs used one model for both), and the collector did not see the
# rows.
# The list named 15 rows. Both transcribers left out aisc360-22/J4.1-splice and said why: this edition
# states no limit on the effective net area of a bolted splice plate. The list had it from an earlier
# edition, so its line is gone from the list below. Both also left out the long-slot column of
# Table J3.5, whose cell is a formula, and the conditions a row cannot hold: the type of hole, whether
# the steel is painted, and whether deformation at service load is a design consideration.
# The 14 rows agree in every value. 6 of them have worked examples, 14 in all, and all reproduce.
# The other 8 have none: the Design Examples never state those limits with numbers.
# Of 100 wrong rows made by one change, the check with no second transcription refused 46. Five of
# the six rows with an example refused every wrong version, 22 in all, and the sixth 6 of 9. The rows
# with no example refused only what the units or a table's shape catch. So a requirement in prose
# rests on its second transcription. `python bench/formalizer/run.py --rows a3.json --second b3.json --examples examples3.json`
# prints this.
# id
column4: its inputs, by the standard's symbols
